questions.title: What annotations are combined by @SpringBootApplication?
explanation: @SpringBootApplication combines Boot configuration, component scanning, and auto-configuration. Keeping it in a root package gives scanning and auto-configuration packages a predictable boundary.

questions.title: Why should a Spring Boot main class usually live in a root package?
explanation: The main class defines the default search package for components, entities, and repositories. A root location covers the application while avoiding accidental scanning of unrelated libraries or the default package.

questions.title: How can the condition evaluation report explain missing auto-configuration?
explanation: Run with debug enabled or inspect the conditions endpoint in an appropriately secured Actuator setup. Positive and negative matches show which class, bean, property, resource, or web-application condition caused an auto-configuration to apply or back off.

questions.title: When should an auto-configuration be excluded?
explanation: Exclude an auto-configuration only when the application deliberately replaces or does not support that feature and normal back-off conditions cannot express the choice. Prefer defining the relevant bean or property first because exclusions couple code to auto-configuration class names.

questions.title: What is the difference between @Configuration and proxyBeanMethods=false?
explanation: Full @Configuration proxying intercepts direct @Bean method calls so they resolve managed singleton instances. With proxyBeanMethods=false, methods behave as ordinary Java calls; it is suitable when bean methods are independent and dependencies arrive through parameters.

questions.title: Why should configuration property classes be validated at startup?
explanation: Bean Validation constraints on @ConfigurationProperties fail startup when required values are missing or malformed. This turns a latent production failure into an immediate deployment error with a property-oriented diagnostic.

questions.title: How does relaxed binding map environment variables to configuration properties?
explanation: Spring Boot normalizes common property-name forms so canonical kebab-case properties can bind from camel case, underscores, and uppercase environment variables. Environment variable names generally replace dots with underscores, remove dashes, and use uppercase.

questions.title: Why did this environment variable fail to bind to a list element?
explanation: List indices in environment variables are surrounded by underscores. A property such as app.servers[0].host maps to APP_SERVERS_0_HOST; a visually similar name without the index separators does not follow Boot's binding rules.

questions.title: How does Spring Boot decide which property value wins?
explanation: Boot applies a documented PropertySource order so later sources override earlier ones. Command-line, test, system, environment, and config-data values can therefore replace defaults; teams should document intended override points and inspect the Environment when results surprise them.

questions.title: When should profile groups be used?
explanation: A profile group gives one business-facing profile a set of finer-grained profiles, such as production activating database, messaging, and observability variants. It reduces launch-time mistakes without hiding secrets or replacing explicit configuration ownership.

questions.title: What is the difference between spring.config.import and profile-specific files?
explanation: Profile-specific files vary local configuration by active profile. spring.config.import composes additional documents or external stores into config data and can mark locations optional; imports are processed with defined precedence relative to their declaring document.

questions.title: Why should secrets not be committed in application.yml?
explanation: Bundled configuration is copied, cached, and distributed with the artifact and repository history. Inject secrets from an access-controlled secret store or deployment environment, rotate them independently, and ensure diagnostics do not expose resolved values.

questions.title: What is the purpose of configuration metadata?
explanation: Configuration metadata describes property names, types, defaults, and documentation for tooling. The configuration processor can generate it from @ConfigurationProperties classes, improving completion and catching misspelled settings during development.

questions.title: When should ApplicationRunner be preferred over CommandLineRunner?
explanation: Both run after startup context creation. ApplicationRunner receives parsed option and non-option arguments, while CommandLineRunner receives the raw String array. Startup tasks should be ordered deliberately, idempotent where possible, and fail startup if their failure makes the service unusable.

questions.title: What is an ApplicationReadyEvent appropriate for?
explanation: ApplicationReadyEvent signals that runners have completed and the application is ready to service requests. It is useful for readiness-adjacent notifications or measurements, but slow critical initialization should remain part of startup rather than creating a falsely ready service.

questions.title: How does constructor injection make a Spring component easier to test?
explanation: Required dependencies become explicit constructor arguments, can be final, and can be supplied directly in a unit test without starting Spring. The object cannot be constructed in a partially injected state.

questions.title: How should multiple beans of the same interface be disambiguated?
explanation: Use @Qualifier for semantic selection, @Primary for a sensible default, or inject a collection/map when all implementations participate. Parameter names can assist resolution, but an explicit qualifier is clearer for important business choices.

questions.title: What lifecycle problem can @Lazy hide?
explanation: Lazy initialization postpones bean creation and may reduce startup work, but it can defer missing dependencies, invalid configuration, or constructor failures until the first request. Use it intentionally and cover the lazy path with readiness or integration tests.

questions.title: What is the difference between @PostConstruct and InitializingBean?
explanation: Both provide initialization callbacks after dependency population. @PostConstruct avoids coupling domain code to Spring interfaces, while InitializingBean is framework-specific; for external configuration, an explicit @Bean init method can keep lifecycle wiring outside the class.

questions.title: Why can request-scoped state not be stored in a singleton bean field?
explanation: Singleton beans are shared across concurrent requests, so mutable request data in a field races and leaks between users. Keep request values local, pass them explicitly, or inject a properly scoped dependency through a proxy when scope semantics require it.

questions.title: How do JDK and class-based Spring AOP proxies differ?
explanation: JDK proxies implement target interfaces; class-based proxies subclass the target. Final classes or methods cannot be advised by subclassing, and proxy calls still require invocation through the proxy rather than self-invocation.

questions.title: Why might @Async execute synchronously when called from the same class?
explanation: Default @Async support is proxy-based. A direct self-call never crosses the proxy, so the interceptor does not submit the work to an executor. Move the asynchronous boundary to another bean or redesign the collaboration.

source.title: Annotation Support for Scheduling and Asynchronous Execution

questions.title: How should the executor behind @Async be sized?
explanation: Size and bound the executor from task behavior, downstream capacity, memory, and latency goals. CPU work needs limited concurrency; blocking work may allow more threads, but an unbounded queue hides overload and increases latency, so define rejection and monitoring policies.

questions.title: What risk does @Scheduled fixedRate create for a slow task?
explanation: Fixed rate measures from scheduled start times and can pressure the scheduler when work takes longer than the interval, especially with a multi-thread scheduler. Choose fixed delay, prevent overlap, or use durable distributed scheduling when exactly-once or cluster coordination matters.

questions.title: When should Spring application events be avoided?
explanation: Events are helpful for decoupled in-process notifications but can hide critical control flow, ordering, transaction, and failure semantics. Use an explicit call for mandatory work and durable messaging or an outbox when delivery must survive process failure.

questions.title: How does @TransactionalEventListener relate an event to a transaction?
explanation: It binds listener execution to a transaction phase such as after commit, preventing a success action from running when the transaction rolls back. It is still in-process delivery and does not by itself guarantee durable publication after a crash.

questions.title: What does @ConditionalOnMissingBean enable in custom auto-configuration?
explanation: It supplies a default bean only when the user has not provided a matching bean, allowing application configuration to override the auto-configuration non-invasively. Conditions should be evaluated after relevant user definitions and documented as part of the starter contract.

questions.title: Why should an auto-configuration not rely on component scanning?
explanation: Auto-configuration should declare imports and beans explicitly so activation remains predictable and isolated from the consuming application's package layout. Scanning can accidentally discover internal components or vary with where the application class lives.

questions.title: How should custom starter dependencies be separated from auto-configuration?
explanation: A conventional project separates an autoconfigure module containing conditional configuration from a starter module that provides a convenient dependency set. This keeps optional technology references isolated and lets advanced consumers use auto-configuration without the opinionated bundle.

questions.title: Why use ObjectProvider for an optional or lazily resolved dependency?
explanation: ObjectProvider can obtain zero, one, or ordered multiple candidates on demand without forcing eager resolution. It is useful in infrastructure code, though normal application services are clearer when required dependencies remain direct constructor arguments.

questions.title: What is the difference between @Controller and @RestController?
explanation: @Controller participates in MVC and normally resolves view names unless methods add @ResponseBody. @RestController composes @Controller and @ResponseBody, so return values are written through message converters by default.

questions.title: How does Spring MVC choose an HttpMessageConverter?
explanation: It considers the Java value or parameter type, request Content-Type, acceptable response media types, and registered converters. Missing or incorrect media headers can therefore produce unsupported-media-type or not-acceptable responses even when routing succeeds.

questions.title: Why should a REST endpoint declare produced media types?
explanation: Declaring produces documents the representation contract and participates in content negotiation, preventing a handler from being selected for an unsupported Accept header. Versioning and error formats still need an application-wide policy.

questions.title: What problem does this @Valid annotation solve?
explanation: @Valid asks MVC to validate the deserialized request object before controller logic runs. Constraint failures become framework validation exceptions that should be rendered through a consistent error contract; validation does not replace domain invariants or authorization.

questions.title: When should @Validated be used instead of @Valid?
explanation: @Valid triggers standard cascaded Bean Validation. Spring's @Validated can additionally select validation groups and enable proxy-based method validation on service types; MVC also has built-in method validation rules that should not be accidentally doubled by a controller proxy.

questions.title: How should REST errors be centralized in Spring MVC?
explanation: Use @RestControllerAdvice or a ResponseEntityExceptionHandler subclass to map expected exceptions to a stable ProblemDetail-based contract. Preserve safe machine codes and correlation data, log server context once, and avoid exposing stack traces or secrets.

questions.title: What is ProblemDetail used for in a Spring REST API?
explanation: ProblemDetail models an RFC-style error response with status, type, title, detail, instance, and extensible properties. A consistent factory or advice layer can add application codes and trace identifiers without inventing different shapes per controller.

questions.title: Why can returning a JPA entity directly from a controller cause problems?
explanation: Serialization can expose internal fields, traverse bidirectional relationships, trigger lazy queries, and couple the public API to persistence mappings. Map entities to explicit request and response models at the application boundary.

questions.title: How should a Spring API paginate a large, frequently changing result set?
explanation: Apply a maximum page size and allow-listed stable sort. Offset pagination is simple but becomes expensive and can shift under concurrent changes; keyset pagination uses the last stable sort key as a cursor for predictable next-page queries. Return navigation metadata without issuing an unnecessary total count when the contract does not need one.

questions.title: What is the difference between a servlet Filter and HandlerInterceptor?
explanation: A Filter runs at the servlet container boundary and can wrap requests or responses before MVC. A HandlerInterceptor runs within MVC around handler execution and can inspect the selected handler; neither replaces method security or controller advice for domain errors.

questions.title: When is WebClient preferable to RestClient?
explanation: WebClient is non-blocking and supports reactive streaming and composition. RestClient offers synchronous fluent calls suited to blocking MVC or imperative code. Choose based on the application's end-to-end execution model rather than using reactive APIs around blocking dependencies.

questions.title: Why must outbound HTTP calls have timeouts?
explanation: Without connection and response deadlines, stalled dependencies consume threads, connections, or reactive demand indefinitely. Set bounded timeouts, propagate an overall deadline, limit retries, and expose outcome metrics so failure remains controlled.

questions.title: What happens when blocking code runs on a WebFlux event-loop thread?
explanation: The small event-loop pool cannot process other connections while a thread blocks, so latency and throughput collapse under load. Use non-blocking drivers or isolate unavoidable blocking work on a bounded scheduler with explicit capacity limits.

questions.title: How do Mono and Flux differ?
explanation: Mono represents asynchronous completion with zero or one item; Flux represents zero to many items. Both can complete successfully or with an error and remain lazy until subscribed by the framework or application.

questions.title: How should large multipart uploads be protected?
explanation: Enforce request and part limits, stream rather than buffer large content, validate media and file signatures, generate server-side names, store outside executable paths, scan when required, and authorize access independently of the submitted filename.

questions.title: What does Spring Data derive from a repository method name?
explanation: The repository infrastructure parses supported subject and predicate keywords to build a query from entity property paths. Long or ambiguous names should give way to @Query, specifications, or a custom repository implementation with tests.

questions.title: When should a JPA projection be used?
explanation: Use interface or DTO projections for read use cases that need a stable subset of fields and do not require a managed aggregate. Verify generated SQL because nested properties can still materialize joins and projections are not a universal cure for inefficient queries.

questions.title: Why can Open Session in View hide data-access defects?
explanation: Keeping the persistence context open through web rendering allows lazy loads outside the service transaction, which can create unpredictable N+1 queries and mix database failures into serialization. Fetch required data explicitly and map it within a defined transaction boundary.

questions.title: What is the difference between save and saveAndFlush in Spring Data JPA?
explanation: save makes the entity managed or merged according to its state, while saveAndFlush additionally asks the persistence provider to synchronize pending changes with the database immediately. Flushing does not commit and should not be used as a substitute for correct transaction boundaries.

questions.title: Why does this repository loop create an N+1 query pattern?
explanation: The first query loads orders, then accessing a lazy customer can issue one additional query per order. Fetch the relationship for this use case with an entity graph, fetch join, projection, or purpose-built query and verify using SQL metrics.

questions.title: How does optimistic locking prevent lost updates?
explanation: A version column is included in update conditions. If another transaction changed the row, the version no longer matches and the update fails instead of silently overwriting newer data; the application then decides whether to reject, merge, or retry.

questions.title: When is pessimistic locking justified?
explanation: Pessimistic locks can protect short, highly contended decisions that cannot tolerate retry, but they reduce concurrency and can deadlock. Keep transactions short, lock rows in consistent order, define timeouts, and prefer optimistic concurrency when conflicts are uncommon.

questions.title: What does @Transactional readOnly=true actually guarantee?
explanation: It is a hint that transaction managers, providers, or databases may use for optimization and policy. It is not a portable security boundary that makes objects immutable or universally rejects writes, so correctness must not depend on it alone.

questions.title: How does transaction propagation REQUIRES_NEW differ from REQUIRED?
explanation: REQUIRED joins an existing transaction or starts one. REQUIRES_NEW suspends the current transaction and starts an independent physical transaction, consuming another connection and committing independently; overuse can exhaust pools and violate expected atomicity.

questions.title: Why did a checked exception not roll back this transaction?
explanation: By default, Spring transaction rules roll back on RuntimeException and Error, not every checked exception. Define rollbackFor when the checked failure must abort the unit of work, or translate it to an appropriate unchecked domain exception.

questions.title: Why should remote network calls usually not occur inside a database transaction?
explanation: The transaction holds connections and locks while waiting on an unreliable dependency, increasing contention and coupling rollback to an operation that may already have happened remotely. Separate boundaries and use idempotency, an outbox, or a saga where cross-system consistency is required.

questions.title: What problem does the transactional outbox pattern solve?
explanation: It stores a domain change and an outgoing message record in one local transaction, then a separate publisher delivers the message. This avoids the gap between committing the database and publishing, while consumers and publishers still need idempotency.

questions.title: Why use Flyway or Liquibase rather than Hibernate schema update in production?
explanation: Versioned migrations are reviewable, ordered, repeatable, and auditable across environments. Automatic ORM schema mutation can be ambiguous, destructive, and difficult to coordinate with rolling deployments or data backfills.

questions.title: How should zero-downtime database migrations be sequenced?
explanation: Use expand-and-contract changes: add backward-compatible schema first, deploy code that tolerates old and new forms, backfill safely, switch reads and writes, then remove obsolete structures after every old instance is gone.

questions.title: How should a HikariCP connection pool be sized?
explanation: Base pool size on database capacity, concurrent query demand, transaction duration, and service replicas rather than web-thread count alone. Bound acquisition time, observe pending requests and usage, and reduce slow transactions before adding connections.

questions.title: What happens when a custom SecurityFilterChain bean is defined?
explanation: It replaces Boot's default web access rules and makes the application responsible for authorization, login mechanisms, CSRF decisions, and Actuator protection. Other authentication auto-configuration may remain unless matching user-service or provider beans are supplied.

questions.title: Why should CSRF not be disabled merely because an API returns JSON?
explanation: CSRF risk depends on whether browsers automatically attach credentials such as session cookies, not the response format. Stateless bearer-token APIs may use a different threat model, but cookie-authenticated endpoints need an intentional CSRF defense.

questions.title: How does request authorization differ from method authorization?
explanation: Request rules protect HTTP paths and methods at the filter chain. Method rules protect service operations regardless of entry point and can enforce argument or ownership logic; sensitive invariants often need both layers.

questions.title: Why must password storage use PasswordEncoder?
explanation: Passwords need a slow, salted, adaptive one-way function rather than encryption or fast hashing. Spring Security's delegating encoder records an algorithm identifier so stored hashes can be verified and upgraded as policy evolves.

questions.title: How does a JWT resource server validate a token?
explanation: It verifies the signature with trusted key material and validates claims such as issuer, timestamps, and optionally audience, then maps authorities for authorization. Decoding payload text alone is not authentication.

questions.title: When should opaque token introspection be chosen over local JWT validation?
explanation: Introspection is useful when the authorization server must centrally determine current token activity or tokens are not self-contained. It adds a network dependency and latency, so apply timeouts, resilience, and a policy for authorization-server outages.

questions.title: Why is CORS not an authentication mechanism?
explanation: CORS controls which browser origins may read cross-origin responses. Non-browser clients ignore it, and an allowed origin still needs authentication and authorization; configure exact origins, methods, headers, and credential rules.

questions.title: How should security headers be customized?
explanation: Keep Spring Security's protective defaults, add application-specific policies such as Content-Security-Policy after testing, and change individual headers rather than disabling the whole feature. Header configuration complements secure output handling and transport security.

questions.title: What is the danger of trusting X-Forwarded-* headers from any client?
explanation: Attackers can spoof scheme, host, or client IP when the application accepts forwarding headers without a trusted proxy boundary. Configure the deployment and Boot forwarding strategy together, strip inbound spoofed headers, and accept values only from controlled proxies.

source.title: Running Behind a Front-end Proxy Server

questions.title: How should authorization ownership checks be implemented?
explanation: Load the protected resource within the trusted service boundary and compare its owner or tenant to the authenticated principal, preferably in a reusable policy or method-security expression. Never authorize using an owner ID supplied only by the client.

questions.title: What is the difference between liveness and readiness health groups?
explanation: Liveness answers whether the process should be restarted; it should not depend on external systems that could cause restart storms. Readiness answers whether the instance should receive traffic and may reflect critical startup or dependency conditions.

questions.title: Why should the Actuator env endpoint be tightly controlled?
explanation: Environment and configuration endpoints reveal property names and operational structure and may expose values if sanitization is weakened. Expose only necessary endpoints on a protected management boundary with explicit authorization.

questions.title: How do metrics, logs, and traces complement one another?
explanation: Metrics quantify trends and alert conditions, traces connect latency and failures across request paths, and logs provide detailed event context. Shared trace and correlation identifiers allow movement from a symptom to the relevant operations without logging sensitive payloads.

questions.title: What makes a custom Micrometer metric useful?
explanation: It represents a stable operational or business signal with documented units and low-cardinality tags. Avoid unbounded labels such as user IDs, URLs with identifiers, or exception messages because they create excessive time series and cost.

questions.title: Why is percentiles-histogram configuration a tradeoff?
explanation: Histograms enable aggregatable latency percentile estimates across instances but increase time-series volume. Enable them for selected service-level metrics and buckets rather than every timer, then verify backend cost and accuracy.

questions.title: How should trace sampling be chosen?
explanation: Sampling balances diagnostic coverage against storage and processing cost. Use a documented baseline probability, preserve important error or business traces when the tracing system supports it, and understand that unsampled traces limit individual-request investigation.

questions.title: What should a custom HealthIndicator report?
explanation: Report a bounded, actionable condition that reflects whether the component can fulfill its role. Use strict timeouts and avoid expensive checks; detailed messages should not reveal secrets and public health responses should expose only the necessary status.

questions.title: Why should logging configuration avoid high-cardinality request data?
explanation: Logging unique payloads, tokens, or personal identifiers increases cost, hampers search, and creates privacy and security exposure. Use structured fields with bounded semantics, correlation IDs, redaction, sampling, and retention aligned to purpose.

questions.title: When is a separate management port useful?
explanation: A separate port lets infrastructure apply different network policy, TLS, and exposure to management endpoints. It is not a substitute for endpoint authorization, and health probes must target the correct port without creating a misleading view of application connectivity.

questions.title: How can graceful shutdown affect readiness during deployment?
explanation: A terminating instance should stop receiving new traffic, allow in-flight requests to finish within a bounded grace period, and then close resources. Probe behavior, load-balancer draining, server shutdown timeout, and platform termination grace must be coordinated.

questions.title: What does @SpringBootTest load compared with a test slice?
explanation: @SpringBootTest creates the full Boot application context and can use mock or real server modes. A slice limits configuration to one layer such as MVC or JPA, making focused tests faster while requiring explicit imports for collaborators outside the slice.

questions.title: When should @WebMvcTest be used?
explanation: Use @WebMvcTest to verify controller routing, binding, validation, serialization, advice, and security MVC behavior with service collaborators mocked or imported deliberately. Use a full integration test when filters, persistence, or actual server behavior are essential.

questions.title: What does @DataJpaTest provide?
explanation: It configures a focused JPA test context, repositories, entity scanning, and transactional rollback, usually replacing the DataSource with an embedded database when available. Database-specific behavior still requires tests against the production engine.

questions.title: Why can an H2 integration test pass while PostgreSQL production fails?
explanation: SQL dialects, types, constraints, locking, transaction isolation, case rules, and query plans differ. Use containerized or managed instances of the production database for migration and critical repository tests, reserving in-memory databases for narrow feedback.

questions.title: What does @ServiceConnection do with Testcontainers?
explanation: It lets Boot derive connection details from a supported container and override normal configuration for the test, reducing manual dynamic properties. The container still needs lifecycle and image choices appropriate to the test suite.

questions.title: When should @MockBean-style context replacement be avoided?
explanation: Replacing many beans can create slow, fragile context variants and tests that verify mocks rather than application wiring. Prefer plain unit tests for isolated behavior, focused slices for boundaries, and a smaller number of realistic integration tests.

questions.title: How does @DynamicPropertySource help an integration test?
explanation: It supplies properties whose values are known only after test infrastructure starts, such as a random container port. The static registry callback lazily resolves values into the test Environment before the context uses them.

questions.title: Why should application context caching influence test design?
explanation: Spring reuses contexts with the same configuration, substantially reducing suite time. Excessive unique properties, mocks, profiles, or @DirtiesContext create new cache keys; group tests around stable configurations and dirty a context only when state truly cannot be reset.

questions.title: What should an end-to-end API integration test verify?
explanation: Exercise the real HTTP boundary, security, serialization, validation, transaction, migration, and production database behavior for representative success and failure paths. Keep external services controlled through test instances or protocol-level stubs rather than mocking the controller's internals.

questions.title: How are Boot executable jars launched?
explanation: The Boot packaging plugins create archives with application classes and nested dependencies plus launcher metadata. The launcher builds the runtime class path without unpacking every dependency, allowing java -jar execution.

questions.title: What advantages do layered container images provide?
explanation: Separating dependencies, loader code, snapshots, and application classes lets unchanged layers remain cached across builds and deployments. Combine layers with a minimal runtime, non-root user, immutable artifact, and reproducible dependency policy.

questions.title: How do Cloud Native Buildpacks differ from a hand-written Dockerfile?
explanation: Buildpacks detect the application and assemble maintained builder and run images with dependency layers and metadata. A Dockerfile gives direct control but makes the team responsible for base images, patching, users, layering, and reproducibility.

questions.title: What changes when building a Spring Boot native image?
explanation: Ahead-of-time processing analyzes the application and generates hints for closed-world native compilation. Startup and footprint can improve, but dynamic reflection, proxies, resources, serialization, and classpath behavior may need hints and native-specific tests.

questions.title: Why must reflection-heavy libraries be tested in a native image?
explanation: Native compilation cannot automatically preserve every class, constructor, method, proxy, or resource reached only dynamically. Runtime hints can register required access, but a successful JVM test does not prove the native executable contains it.

questions.title: How should configuration be supplied to a containerized Boot application?
explanation: Build one immutable image and inject environment-specific config and secrets at deployment through supported external sources. Avoid rebuilding for each environment, validate configuration at startup, and keep secrets out of image layers and command history.

questions.title: What causes a Spring Boot startup failure to be actionable?
explanation: Preserve the earliest meaningful cause, Boot failure analysis, condition report, active profiles, and relevant configuration names while redacting values. A deployment should fail fast when required infrastructure or configuration is invalid rather than remain partially healthy.

questions.title: How should retry be applied to an outbound dependency?
explanation: Retry only transient and idempotent operations, use a small attempt budget with exponential backoff and jitter, honor the caller deadline, and combine with timeouts and concurrency limits. Record attempts separately so retries do not conceal a failing dependency.

questions.title: Why can adding more servlet threads make latency worse?
explanation: If database connections, CPU, or downstream capacity are already saturated, more request threads create queues, context switching, and memory pressure without increasing throughput. Measure each constrained resource and apply bounded concurrency and backpressure.

questions.title: What is the value of reproducible Boot builds?
explanation: Reproducible archives remove timestamp and ordering variation so identical inputs produce identical artifacts. This improves caching, provenance comparison, and incident verification, while dependency locking and trusted build environments address additional supply-chain concerns.

questions.title: What production evidence should be collected before declaring a Spring Boot service ready?
explanation: Run migrations and representative functional, security, concurrency, failure, restart, and load tests against production-like infrastructure. Verify latency percentiles, resource limits, pool saturation, probes, graceful shutdown, alerts, dashboards, backups, rollback, and secret/config delivery rather than relying only on a successful build.
